$comment: The two pages the browser is shown when the loopback redirect lands (HPS-08), pinned as the
copy and the structure rather than as whole documents.
Why it is here and not in each host: the two pages are the same moment in the same flow, and
before this file they did not say the same thing -- one host headed the page 'Signed in' and
the other 'Signed in to Mantle Place', one said 'return to Revit' and the other 'return to the
application'. Nothing failed when they diverged. Fixing one by hand and copying the result into
the other starts them matched and lets them drift again on the next edit, which is how they got
there. HPS-43's share model for two hosts in two languages is specifications plus this corpus,
and this is the specification half.
Whole documents are deliberately NOT pinned. The markup is each host's to write in its own
language, and a byte-for-byte document fixture would fail on an indent. What must not drift is
what the user reads and what the page is allowed to reach for -- so the copy is exact, and the
structure is stated as substrings that must be present and substrings that must be absent.
Exact. A host builds its pages' visible text from these and nothing else.
`closing` carries the one legitimate per-host difference, and it is a substitution rather
than a fork: `hostNames` is keyed by the bundle manifest's hosts.<hostId> ids, the same
vocabulary the `?host=` sign-in parameter uses. A host reads the whole map, not just its own
row, so adding a third host here is a red test in the two that already exist rather than a
silent omission.
copy.successBody: You're signed in to Mantle Place.
copy.closing: You can close this tab and return to {hostName}.

$comment: As MantlePlacePalette states it for the Unreal editor UI, so one palette covers the plugin
chrome and these pages. Dark is the fix rather than a preference: the platform's own hand-off
page is dark, and arriving from it onto default white read as something having gone wrong.
Stated as whole CSS declarations rather than as bare colours, for two reasons. It is what a
host must actually emit -- a page shipping the value in a comment and rendering default white
passes a bare-colour check and fails this one. And ci-public-hygiene exempts a hex triplet
only where a colon precedes it, which a CSS declaration provides and a bare quoted value does
not; writing the declaration satisfies that exemption honestly rather than widening it.
Present on BOTH pages, absent from BOTH pages. The `lacks` list is HPS-08 stated as the
absence of every way to reach off-page for something the renderer NEEDS: the browser may have
no network by the time the redirect lands, and a page that reaches for a stylesheet renders as
unstyled text. The hand-off below is not one of these -- it is a navigation the page survives
failing.
The closing line is on the failure page too: HPS-08 asks each of them to tell the user to
close the tab, and the failure page is where a curator left staring at a dead tab goes looking
for a button that is not there.
The success page probes the platform's branded completion page and navigates only if
something answered.
A <meta http-equiv="refresh"> would navigate unconditionally, so with no network the browser
would land on its own 'can't reach this site' page and the branded page would have been
rendered and thrown away in exactly the case it exists for. Probe-then-navigate inverts that:
no response, no navigation, and the curator keeps looking at a complete page on brand. The
hand-off is an upgrade, never a dependency, which is what keeps it inside HPS-08's 'small
self-contained HTML page' rather than beside it.
`successOnly` is load-bearing. The failure page interpolates an error_description the
authorization server wrote; keeping that string off any page that executes anything leaves
the escape pass as the only thing that has to be right about it. `failurePageLacks` is how
that is checked rather than trusted.
HPS-08's ordering, restated here as vectors because this is the file the page copy lives in
and the two are edited together. Escaping '<' first would produce < and the later '&' pass
would double-escape it to &lt;, which renders as literal '<' on the page. The message
can carry an error_description the authorization server wrote, so it is not the host's to
trust.
The FIRST vector is the one that catches a reversed order. Run '<', then '&', then '>' over
it and the '<' it just wrote comes back as '&lt;' -- a different string, so the vector
fails. The third vector is a different trap: input that is already an entity must come out
escaped once more, not left alone.
